sentences.text: We describe a repository-based research system that connects questions, proofs, computations and failed approaches to reviewed claims and publications.

sentences.text: A research repository must support several activities: choosing a question, recovering earlier work, testing an argument, reviewing a claim and publishing an explanation. Their outputs need to remain connected when a proof, experiment or manuscript changes. Otherwise a new contributor must reconstruct the history, and a correct result can acquire a misleading description.
sentences.warrant: Motivates keeping research artifacts and their revision relationships together; no frequency or performance estimate.

sentences.text: Plectis is the public repository prototype studied here. It keeps questions, prior sources, computations, proofs and unresolved steps together, with records of proposed contributions and their review. Its implemented scope is the research and publication workflow in this repository; broader autonomous discovery and services for other scientific fields are proposals (Section~\ref{sec:limits}).

sentences.text:
\subsection{Stored artifacts and executable tools}
The checkout contains authored Lean and manuscript sources, JSON records for selected claims and their evidence, and a journal of research returns. Indexes, source coordinates and status summaries are derived from those records. Authors edit the sources; builders regenerate the derived views. This division gives a reviewer a source to inspect when a generated view changes. In reviewing a claim, the maintainer must still distinguish a finite computation's tested range from a general theorem, or a failed attempt from an argument that every approach must fail. The \repolink{docs/ARCHITECTURE.md}{architecture guide} identifies the source files and their derived views.
sentences.warrant: The ownership distinction is stated as source versus derived view. Mathematical scope remains a maintainer review responsibility rather than an automated inference from an index.

The command-line tools have bounded jobs:
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{2.55cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
Component & Input, output and responsibility\\
\midrule
Task routing & \repolink{scripts/agent_entry.py}{agent\_entry.py} maps a stated task to instructions, relevant files and commands; the researcher chooses the question and approach.\\[3pt]
Evidence retrieval & \repolink{scripts/query_corpus.py}{query\_corpus.py} returns problem, claim, declaration and paper-source records from the indexes.\\[3pt]
Proof sessions & \repolink{scripts/proof_workbench.py}{proof\_workbench.py} records notes and submitted Lean probes, derives verdicts from the Lean process, and binds a session claim to an accepted probe.\\[3pt]
Statement evidence & \repolink{scripts/paper_evidence.py}{paper\_evidence.py} resolves mathematical paper statements against source and verification records; \repolink{scripts/paper_claim_evidence.py}{paper\_claim\_evidence.py} projects their evidence status and reported gaps.\\[3pt]
Editorial exchange & \repolink{scripts/short_paper_writer.py}{short\_paper\_writer.py} audits manuscripts and packages proposed revisions without applying or approving the return.\\[3pt]
Research history & \repolink{scripts/research_record.py}{research\_record.py} verifies the journal of entered returns and dispositions and reports what recorded outputs still owe.\\[3pt]
Derived views & \repolink{scripts/refresh_projections.py}{refresh\_projections.py} runs builders in dependency order; \repolink{scripts/check_release.py}{check\_release.py} checks release contracts and freshness.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}
A separate self-audit, \repolink{scripts/systems_paper_evidence.py}{systems\_paper\_evidence.py}, checks this systems manuscript's text and cited source bindings. These are inspectable software responsibilities, not measurements of research quality or new execution results.

A human or agent chooses the next task and invokes these tools; recording the sequence does not make the workbench an autonomous search policy.

sentences.text:
\subsection{Researcher, agent and maintainer responsibilities}
A researcher chooses the task and the evidence needed to answer it. A coding agent can inspect files, invoke tools and prepare a proposed change using the public instructions; ordinary written arguments and explanations can also be contributed without a clone or an agent. A maintainer reviews the claim, attribution and remaining uncertainty before adoption. The contributor and reviewer may be the same agent, so this division of responsibilities does not establish independent review. Public setup and review instructions are in the \repolink{docs/agents/README.md}{agent quickstart} and \repolink{CONTRIBUTING.md}{contribution guide}.
sentences.warrant: Public file/terminal agent instructions and ordinary submissions coexist. Maintainer review remains a responsibility and can share the actor.

sentences.text: A typical iteration starts with a question and the recorded work that bears on it. The researcher investigates, then returns an argument, experiment, correction or manuscript change with its evidence and limitations. Review may adopt it, request revision, defer it or reject it. Accepted work changes the authored claims, papers and evidence records; builders and release checks update the dependent views before the next task uses them. The journal preserves dispositions for the structured returns explicitly entered into it. Ordinary issues, pull requests and ideas can enter review without a journal session. Sections~\ref{sec:paper} and~\ref{sec:contribute} give the implemented publication exchange and the wider contribution procedure.
sentences.warrant: Candidate return -> maintainer review -> authored claims/papers/evidence -> builders/checks. Journal scope explicitly entered; ordinary issue/PR remains available.

sentences.text: The worked case concerns a theorem about infinite sums of reciprocals over a restricted set of positive integer exponents. A base-two weighted convergence condition restricts the allowable sets; under it, every infinite subset gives an irrational sum at every integer base at least two. Removing the condition would assert a solution of a more general problem that remains open. Appendix~\ref{app:worked-proof} gives the exact statement and calculation.
sentences.warrant: Accurate informal description of the existing weighted-support theorem: positive exponents, base-two weighted convergence, every infinite subset and every integer base at least two. The hypothesis is part of a proved implication, not a named unproved input; arbitrary support remains open. Type A integration shortens the example for laboratory infrastructure readers; the same source relation and evidence ceiling are retained.

In \repolink{docs/paper_lean_coverage.json}{paper\_lean\_coverage.json}, a row identifies the weighted-support theorem's occurrence in the mathematical paper, its statement digest, source location and two Lean supports. A separate \repolink{docs/systems_paper_sentences.json}{sentence ledger} binds this systems paper's explanation to specified source passages and an authored rationale. For example, the appendix's hereditary conclusion is bound to both the ordinary proof and its formal declaration. These records make the two correspondences inspectable; deciding whether the explanation preserves the condition remains a review task.
sentences.warrant: The native coverage row contains the paper/label identity, statement digest, source coordinate and both declarations. The existing sentence unit r4.example4.08 is bound to r8-weighted-proof and r8-hereditary-formal. This describes those two extant record types, not a new join or replay; the supplemental return audit checks this local pointer. Type A integration shortens the example for laboratory infrastructure readers; the same source relation and evidence ceiling are retained.

One gives fixed-base irrationality and the all-base conclusion for every infinite subset; the other makes the fixed-base hereditary conclusion explicit. Their roles overlap. sentences.text:
\paragraph{Balancing the two costs.}
The modulus must cancel $F$ while making the remaining exponents amenable to one of two estimates. Fix a positive common multiple $L$ of~$F$, put $p_*=\max P$, and, for $H\ge2p_*$, set
\[
 Q=L\prod_{p\in P}p^{\lfloor\log_p H\rfloor},\qquad
 G=\lfloor H/p_*\rfloor.
\]
If $h_P(a)\le H$, then $h_P(a)\mid Q$. Since $n/(b^n-1)$ decreases for positive integers~$n$, the complete-cycle term in~\eqref{eq:worked-orbit} is bounded by $h_P(a)/[a(b^{h_P(a)}-1)]$. Its sum outside~$F$ is less than $\varepsilon$.

If $h_P(a)>H$, then $\gcd(a,Q)\ge G$: either every $P$-prime-power component of $h_P(a)$ is at most $H$, so $h_P(a)\mid Q$, or one exceeds $H$, and its truncated component in $Q$ is greater than $H/p_*\ge G$. Summing~\eqref{eq:worked-orbit} over these exponents up to $QT$ costs at most
\[
 \frac{G(1+\log(QT))+Q}{b^G-1}:
\]
the harmonic sum supplies $1+\log(QT)$, and at most $QT$ unfinished-cycle terms supply~$Q$.

Increasing $M$ therefore has two effects. It reduces the first group's unfinished-cycle cost $Q/M$, but increases the second group's cost through $\log T<2M\log2$. We need both $Q/M\to0$ and $GM/b^G\to0$, not merely a long average. With $F$ and $L$ fixed, $Q\le LH^{|P|}$ and $G=H/p_*+O(1)$. The choice $M=\lfloor b^{G/2}\rfloor$ meets both requirements.

The source proof combines these estimates into the finite mean
\begin{equation}\label{eq:worked-mean}
\begin{aligned}
 &\frac1M\sum_{j=M}^{2M-1}\frac1{2^j}
       \sum_{t=1}^{2^j}\Delta_{b,A}(tQ)\\
 &\qquad\le \varepsilon+\frac{2QW_{b,P}(A)}M
       +\frac{G(1+\log Q+2M\log2)+Q}{b^G-1}+4\,2^{-M}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The terms bound, respectively, the weighted tail over complete cycles, its unfinished cycles, the exponents with large gcd, and the exponents beyond $QT$. The second term uses~\eqref{eq:worked-dyadic} with $\alpha_a=\mathbf1_A(a)/(b^{h_P(a)}-1)$; the last uses the geometric tail bound $4/T$. After $\varepsilon$, $F$ and $L$ have been fixed, every term after $\varepsilon$ tends to zero as $H\to\infty$~\cite[Section~2, weighted-support proof]{paper257}.

The left side of~\eqref{eq:worked-mean} is an average with nonnegative weights summing to one: each length has weight $1/M$, distributed equally among its $2^j$ terms. For large $H$, at least one displacement is therefore less than $2\varepsilon$. Taking $0<\varepsilon<1/(2q)$ contradicts the lower bound $1/q$. This argument gives no rate of decay in~$N$. Passing to an infinite $B\subseteq A$ only decreases the weighted sum, and $b^{h_P(a)}-1\ge2^{h_P(a)}-1$ gives the all-base conclusion from the binary hypothesis~\cite[Section~2]{paper257}.
sentences.warrant: Clarifies normalized finite weights and epsilon choice; no selected-index rate of decay and no stronger hereditary conclusion.
